explain.title: Decimal uses base 10
explain.body: The decimal number system is a base-10 number system that consists of digit from 0 to 9 and we use it in everyday life. That's why each digit of the number represents a power of 10. In the decimal system the place values starting from the rightmost digits are 10⁰, 10¹, 10², and so on. For example, 523 = 5 × 10² + 2 × 10¹ + 3 × 10⁰ = 523.

explain.title: Binary uses base 2
explain.body: In binary, the place values are arranged from the right to left, starting with 2⁰, and ending at 2ⁿ,where each position represents a power of 2. Binary digits are 0 and 1. Computers use binary because digital circuits have two states: on and off, represented by 1 and 0.

explain.title: Octal uses base 8
explain.body: Octal is a positional numeral system with base eight, which implies that a digit to be used ranges from 0 to 7. The last digit is a single digit power of 8 while the other digits are the coefficients. In the decimal system, the place values starting from the 8⁰, 8¹, 8² and so on. Each octal digit represents three binary digits (bits) because 8 = 2³.

explain.title: Hexadecimal uses base 16
explain.body: The hexadecimal is a base 16 number system with digit number from 0 to 9 and alphabets from A to F; each digit represents 16 to the power of the position of the digit. The letter A to F stand for the numeric value of 10 to 15. Since 16 = 2⁴, each hexadecimal digit corresponds to four binary bits.

explain.title: Convert by repeated division
explain.body: To convert a decimal number to binary, octal, or hexadecimal, repeatedly divide by 2, 8, or 16 respectively. Record each remainder, continue until the quotient is 0, then read the remainders from bottom to top.

explain.title: Signed integers
explain.body: Integers extend the concept of whole numbers to include negative numbers. In computer programming, we call them signed integers. One bit is reserved as the sign bit (the most significant bit). For n bits, the maximum positive value is 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1.

explain.title: ASCII
explain.body: ASCII is an acronym that stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange. It is a character encoding standard adopted for representing in devices such as computers and similar systems that use text. Each alphabet, number or symbol is given a code number between 0 and 127.

explain.title: Extended ASCII

explain.title: Unicode
explain.body: Unicode is an attempt at mapping all graphic characters used in any of the world's writing system. Unlike ASCII, which is limited to 7bits and can represent only 128 characters, Unicode can represent over a million characters through different forms of encodings such as, UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32.

explain.title: UTF encoding forms

explain.title: Files are stored as binary data

explain.title: Characters and codes
explain.body: ASCII gives binary codes to a limited set of text characters. Unicode gives code points to characters from many languages and writing systems.

explain.title: Integers in memory
explain.body: Integers are stored as bits. Unsigned integers represent zero and positive values; signed integers can represent negative values, commonly using two's complement.

explain.title: Bit count and number range
explain.body: More bits allow more possible values. An unsigned integer with n bits ranges from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.

explain.title: Floating-point numbers
explain.body: Single precision uses 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 fraction bits. It represents a wide range of values, but its precision and range are limited.

explain.title: Binary arithmetic and images
explain.body: Binary numbers can be added, subtracted, multiplied, and divided using place values and carries. Images are made of pixels; RGB means Red, Green, Blue.

mistakes: Using the digit 2 or another non-binary digit in a binary number.

notes.title: Numbering Systems: Bases and Conversion
notes.answer: The number systems in this section are decimal (base 10), binary (base 2), octal (base 8), and hexadecimal (base 16).
notes.explanation: A number system uses a base to decide its place values and which digits are allowed. To convert from decimal, divide by the new base and read the remainders from bottom to top. To convert a binary number to decimal, add the place values of its 1s.
notes.simple: A base tells you how many different digit values a number system uses. For example, binary uses only 0 and 1, while octal uses 0 through 7.
steps: Identify the base you are converting from and the base you are converting to.
For decimal to binary, octal or hexadecimal, divide repeatedly by 2, 8 or 16, respectively.
Write down each remainder and continue until the quotient is 0.
Read the remainders from bottom to top.
For binary to decimal, multiply each digit by its place value and add the results.

notes.title: Storing whole numbers and integers
notes.explanation: An unsigned 2-byte whole number uses 16 bits. Its values range from 0 to 2¹⁶ − 1, which is 65,535.
notes.simple: More bits let a computer store a wider range of whole-number values. Signed integers can be negative; unsigned whole numbers cannot.
examples: An unsigned 1-byte whole number ranges from 0 to 255.
An 8-bit signed integer ranges from −128 to 127.
steps: A byte has 8 bits, so 2 bytes have 16 bits.
For an unsigned number, the minimum value is 0.
Find the maximum using 2ⁿ − 1: 2¹⁶ − 1 = 65,535.

notes.title: Storing Real Values in Computer Memory
notes.answer: A floating-point value is represented using a sign bit, an exponent, and a mantissa.
notes.explanation: A real number with a fractional part can be written in binary and stored using a sign bit, an exponent, and a mantissa. To convert a decimal fraction to binary, repeatedly multiply it by 2 and record each integer part.
notes.simple: Computers store decimal numbers with fractions by expressing them in binary and dividing their storage into parts.
steps: Separate the number into its integer and fractional parts.
To convert a fractional part to binary, multiply it by 2.
Record the integer part of each result, from top to bottom.
Continue with each new fractional part until it reaches zero or the required precision is achieved.
For single precision, use 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 mantissa bits.
notes.checkQuestion: What are the three main components used to represent a floating-point value?
notes.checkAnswer: The sign bit, exponent, and mantissa.

notes.title: Binary Arithmetic Operations
notes.answer: Binary addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are performed using the digits 0 and 1 and the rules for each operation.
notes.explanation: Binary arithmetic uses the digits 0 and 1. Addition uses carries; subtraction can be done by adding the subtrahend's two's complement; multiplication and division follow familiar decimal methods using binary digits.
notes.simple: Work with just 0 and 1. For subtraction, change the subtrahend to its two's complement, add it, and discard the final carry.
steps: For addition, add the bits from right to left and carry 1 when needed.
For subtraction, invert the subtrahend's bits and add 1.
Add the minuend and the two's complement.
Discard the carry bit if one appears.
For multiplication and division, use the familiar long-operation steps with binary digits.

notes.title: Common Text Encoding Schemes
notes.answer: ASCII represents characters using code numbers from 0 to 127. Unicode maps graphic characters used in the world's writing systems and can be encoded in forms such as UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32.
notes.explanation: ASCII assigns a number to each character. Unicode can represent characters from many writing systems, and UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32 are ways of encoding Unicode characters.
notes.simple: Encoding gives characters a computer-readable form, such as a number or a sequence of bits.
steps: Identify the character.
Look up its code or Unicode code point.
Use the encoding scheme to represent it in binary.
State how many bits or bytes the encoding uses, when required.
notes.checkQuestion: How many bits does standard ASCII use?
notes.checkAnswer: ASCII uses 7 bits and can represent 128 characters.

notes.title: How computers store images, audio, and video
notes.answer: Images use pixels and RGB colour values; audio uses sampling and quantization; videos use frames. Computers store all of them as binary data.
notes.explanation: Images are made from pixels. Each pixel has a colour, represented in a colour image by Red, Green, and Blue (RGB) values. Computers store image, audio, and video files as binary data: sequences of 0s and 1s.
notes.simple: A digital picture is made from tiny coloured dots. A computer stores the information about those dots using 0s and 1s.
examples: A pixel with RGB values (255, 0, 0) is bright red.
A video frame rate tells how many frames are shown each second.
steps: Identify whether the file is an image, audio, or video.
For an image, think of pixels and their RGB colour values.
For audio, remember sampling and quantization.
For video, remember that frames are shown in sequence and measured in frames per second.
Remember that all these files are stored as binary data.

notes.title: How computers represent information
notes.explanation: This unit covers how computers represent text, integers, floating-point numbers, and images. It also practises binary arithmetic and signed 4-bit calculations.
notes.simple: A computer stores information as bits: 0s and 1s. Different rules let those bits represent letters, numbers, and pictures.
examples: Unsigned 2-byte integers use 16 bits, so their range is 0 to 2¹⁶ − 1, or 0 to 65,535.
In 4-bit two's complement, −5 is made by writing 5 as 0101, inverting the bits to 1010, then adding 1 to get 1011.
steps: For an unsigned integer with n bits, use the range 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.
For a signed 4-bit value, use two's complement: invert the positive number's bits and add 1 to represent its negative.
For binary addition and subtraction, line up the bits and work from right to left, carrying or borrowing as needed.
Unicode assigns code points to characters from many languages.
An image is made of pixels, and RGB represents colour using red, green, and blue.

written.text: Q2.2. Describe in detail how integers are stored in computer memory.
modelAnswer: Computer memory stores an integer as a pattern of binary bits, each having a value of 0 or 1.
The number of bits allocated to the integer determines how many different values can be stored.
For an unsigned n-bit integer, all bit patterns represent non-negative values, from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.
A signed integer must also represent negative values.
A common signed representation is two's complement.
To form a negative value in two's complement, write the positive value in binary, invert its bits, and add 1.
For example, in 4 bits, 5 is 0101; invert to get 1010 and add 1 to get 1011, which represents −5.
Thus, the same bit pattern is interpreted according to whether the integer is signed or unsigned.

Q2.3. Explain the process of converting a decimal integer to its binary representation and vice versa. Include examples of both positive and
negative integers.
modelAnswer: To convert a positive decimal integer to binary, divide by 2 repeatedly and record each remainder.
Read the remainders from bottom to top.
To convert binary to decimal, multiply each bit by its power-of-2 place value and add: 1101₂ = 1 × 8 + 1 × 4 + 0 × 2 + 1 × 1 = 13₁₀.
For a negative integer, use a fixed number of bits and two's complement.
In 4 bits, 5 is 0101; invert the bits to get 1010 and add 1 to get 1011.
Therefore, −5₁₀ = 1011₂ in 4-bit two's complement; conversely, 1011₂ represents −5₁₀.
